Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The narrative primarily unfolds as a vivid, real-time scene—Arthur discovering the car crash, calling the dispatcher, and waiting beside the deceased woman until emergency services arrive. Rather than interrupting this scene with dry blocks of exposition, the author cleverly integrates Arthur's backstory and internal summary (his career as an actuary, the death of his brother, and the failure of his marriage) directly into the real-time action through his spoken monologue to the woman and brief, triggered memories. This balance keeps the immediate tension and sensory grounding of the ravine intact while providing all the necessary character history to make Arthur's emotional realization at the end impactful.
